History:
• 31-year-old male with 4-day history of intensely pruritic, red, sore rash on chest, hands, and antecubital fossae.  
• Rash is dry with areas of skin cracking; no bleeding, pus, or discharge.  
• Pruritus severe—interferes with sleep, concentration at work, and leisure activities (e.g., hiking).  
• No fever, systemic symptoms, respiratory complaints, or urinary/bowel changes.  
• No known new exposures to soaps, detergents, or clothing; no clear trigger identified.  
• Previous eczema limited to arms; current episode more widespread and pruritic.  
• Tried OTC steroid cream (name/dose not documented) last night and OTC antihistamines without relief.

Past Medical History:
• Atopic dermatitis (eczema) – prior episodes.  
• Asthma (childhood, currently inactive).  
• Allergies: None reported.  
• Medications: None regular. Recent OTC topical steroid (dose/route/frequency not documented) and OTC antihistamines (name/dose/frequency not documented).

Physical Examination:
(Remote video assessment)  
• Erythematous, dry, excoriated plaques with superficial cracking over chest, dorsal hands, and antecubital areas.  
• No vesicles, weeping, pus, or bleeding observed.  
• No facial involvement.  
• Patient alert, oriented, speaking full sentences; no respiratory distress reported.

Impression:
• Likely acute flare of atopic dermatitis (eczema exacerbation).

Management Plan:
• Prescribe higher-potency topical corticosteroid cream/ointment (specific preparation and instructions not documented).  
• Prescribe/emphasize regular use of emollients for bathing and moisturizing.  
• Prescribe oral antihistamine (Fexofenadine; dose/frequency not documented) for pruritus.  
• Advise daily application of steroid and liberal/emollient use for 7–10 days, then reassess efficacy.  
• Recommend diary of possible irritant/allergen triggers (soaps, detergents, fabrics).  
• Counsel on gentle skin care: lukewarm showers, fragrance-free cleansers, avoid scratching, keep nails short.  
• Follow-up: return in one week if no improvement or sooner if worsening or signs of infection (oozing, fever).

Patient Summary:
A 31-year-old man with prior eczema presents with a 4-day, severely itchy, dry, cracked rash over chest, hands, and inner elbows. Clinical picture is consistent with an eczema flare. He will start a stronger topical steroid, emollients, and oral antihistamine, with close follow-up in one week.

Key Takeaways:
1. Apply the prescribed steroid cream and moisturizers consistently for at least 7–10 days.  
2. Take the oral antihistamine to help control itching, especially at night.  
3. Track any products or activities that worsen the rash to identify triggers.

Next Steps:
• Initiate prescribed treatments today.  
• Monitor skin daily for improvement or signs of infection.  
• Schedule follow-up appointment in 1 week; sooner visit if rash spreads, oozes, or systemic symptoms develop.  
• Consider dermatology referral if poor response to therapy.
